problem: Recent object navigation methods use object association only to speed up the 'search for' phase (start to first seeing the target) and neglect the 'navigate to' phase (after seeing the target). End-to-end agents spend ~60% of steps in that phase (humans ~40%) and reach the target only ~80% of the time after seeing it. Modular semantic-map methods handle it but are costly and sensitive to noise.
motivation: Humans switch between associative search thinking and navigational thinking, whereas current agents lose the target from view and repeatedly re-search for it. The paper brings the modular idea of decoupling into an end-to-end network without semantic maps, by keeping a compact memory of target orientation.
key_idea: Dual adaptive thinking: an end-to-end agent combines a search-thinking network (object-association attention) with a navigation-thinking network (a compact target-oriented memory graph refined by a target-aware multi-scale aggregator), fused adaptively according to navigation progress.
insight: Storing only target bounding box, confidence and agent pose (9-D nodes) is far cheaper than storing object or image features (0.64% and 0.29% of the memory at L=40) and gives higher SNE. Ablations show navigation thinking without TAMSA raises SR and SNE but lowers SPL (45.04 to 43.15); TAMSA, adaptive fusion and LayerNorm recover SPL, ending at SR 82.39 / SPL 48.93. Completely separated thinking fails (SR 72.09) because memory is initially insufficient and visual cues for obstacle avoidance are lost, so search thinking must stay active throughout.
method: Search thinking network: uses the DOA graph's object-target association scores to reweight DETR object features and, through multi-head attention, ResNet18 image features; concatenated with previous-action embedding; pretrained by imitation learning.
Target-oriented memory graph (TOMG): stores up to L nearest target-visible nodes (confidence > cf=0.4), each a 9-D vector of target bbox, confidence and agent pose relative to the start; zero-padded.
Egocentric coordinate transformation: converts stored node positions and sin/cos of angles into the current node's frame at each step, giving an L×11 feature.

TAMSA: FC-LN-FC encoding, then three dilated TCNs (d=0,1,2, weighted by w_d) generate dynamic kernels that aggregate L nodes to 3 implicit nodes, with circle padding. Target-semantic channel attention from the one-hot target follows, then flatten, FC and a residual connection.
Adaptive fusion: NT is all zero before the target is seen; afterwards NT and ST are concatenated, layer-normalized and linearly projected, so navigation thinking gradually dominates.
Training: A3C reinforcement learning, with the search network pretrained by imitation and then trained jointly. New SNE metric measures efficiency in the navigate-to phase.

setting.backbone: ResNet18 + DETR features, attention/TCN/FC networks with LSTM-style policy (trained with A3C)
setting.training_data: AI2-THOR: 4 room types × 30 rooms (20 train / 5 val / 5 test per type); RoboTHOR for additional experiments; imitation pretraining of the search network
setting.observation: single-view egocentric RGB (plus DETR detections); agent pose tracked relative to start
setting.action_space: discrete: MoveAhead, RotateLeft, RotateRight, LookDown, LookUp, Done
setting.privileged: none (relative pose estimated from start; target detection via DETR)

results: On AI2-THOR, DAT reaches SR 82.39, SPL 48.93 and SNE 139.83, beating DOA (74.32/40.27/120.86) and VTNet in SR and SPL. Its SNE is slightly below PONI (141.17), but its SPL is much higher (PONI 37.27). On RoboTHOR it reaches SR 41.72 versus DOA 36.22.
limitations: Dual thinking slightly weakens efficiency in the search-for phase because the two thinking modes are coupled during joint training.
Evaluated only in simulated AI2-THOR and RoboTHOR, with no real-robot tests; it depends on target detection and on the accuracy of relative pose estimated from the start.
Pose relative to the start is assumed to be tracked accurately; robustness to odometry noise is not tested.
